figures.alt: Black-and-white photograph of two locomotives nose to nose, surrounded by a large crowd of workers and officials at Promontory Summit, Utah
figures.caption: The golden spike ceremony at Promontory Summit, Utah, May 10, 1869

options.misconception: Background: the government funded the lines with land grants and loans, and federal aid to railroads continued after 1869.
options.text: It shows that the federal government had stopped funding western railroads

options.misconception: Background: railroads brought settlers and soldiers onto Native lands, and Native peoples resisted, as at Little Bighorn in 1876.
options.text: It shows that Native peoples welcomed the railroad across their lands

options.misconception: Background: eastern factories needed western timber, minerals, cattle, and wheat more than ever; the railroad fed them.
options.text: It shows that eastern factories no longer needed western raw materials
It joins railroads, western settlement, and a national market in one scene

rationales.A: Background: the government did not stop funding railroads. Land grants and loans built these lines, and federal support for railroads continued after 1869.
rationales.B: Background: Native peoples did not welcome the railroad. It carried settlers and soldiers onto their lands, and resistance continued, as at Little Bighorn in 1876.
rationales.C: Background: eastern factories needed western goods more than ever. The railroad carried timber, minerals, cattle, and wheat east to feed industry.
rationales.D: One photograph holds the whole period's story: the railroad that tied the continent together, the settlement it carried west, and the single national market it created.
rationales.general:
Think of the golden spike as the period's front door: everything that follows walks through it.
1. List what the railroad set in motion. Settlement rushed west, and eastern factories gained western raw materials.
2. Ask what ties those changes together. A single national market, joined by rail.
3. Name the fitting image. One scene holding railroads, settlement, and the national market at once.
Remember: a period's opening image should hold its biggest forces together, not just one event.

stem: Which of the following best explains why the event in the photograph is a fitting opening image for Period 6 (1865–1898)?

stimulus.source_note: Photograph by A. J. Russell, 1869. Public domain. Wikimedia Commons: https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Golden_Spike_ceremony,_Promontory,_Utah,_May_10,_1869.jpg
stimulus.text: The photograph shows two locomotives nose to nose at Promontory Summit, Utah, on May 10, 1869, surrounded by a crowd of workers and officials celebrating the driving of the golden spike. The Central Pacific line from the west and the Union Pacific line from the east met here, joining the continent by rail.
